Shark vs Dyson Hair Dryer

Shark sits between Laifen and Dyson on price and adds scalp protection — but with only 64 Canadian ratings, its long-term reliability is even less proven than Laifen's.

The short answer: Shark’s SpeedStyle Pro at about C$200 is roughly half the price of a Dyson Supersonic and adds a scalp-protection feature Dyson does not have. That makes it genuinely interesting. But there is a caveat we have to lead with: the Shark SpeedStyle Pro has only 64 Canadian ratings in our dataset, against 310 for the Dyson Supersonic Travel. There are not yet enough long-term Canadian owners to say anything confident about how long it lasts. Dyson has the track record and the service network; Shark has the price and one feature advantage.

One important clarification before you compare prices. Shark’s huge search volume in Canada belongs to the FlexStyle, which is a multi-styler comparable to the Dyson Airwrap — not to a hair dryer. The SpeedStyle Pro is the product that competes with the Supersonic. Comparing FlexStyle to a Supersonic, as plenty of comparison content does, is comparing two different jobs.

Read the ratings count row carefully. Shark’s 64 ratings is a small sample. A 4.4-star average from 64 buyers is far less informative than a 4.4-star average from 310. We would not draw a reliability conclusion from it in either direction.

Price in Canada: Shark vs Dyson

The Shark SpeedStyle Pro at about C$200 undercuts the Dyson Supersonic Travel by 2× and the Nural by 3.2×.

Where the price gap is narrower than you might expect. Compared with Laifen — which sits at roughly a quarter of Dyson pricing — Shark’s half-price positioning leaves less room to be forgiving. At about C$200 you are paying real money, and the case for Shark over a Laifen Air at about C$100 rests on features rather than pure value.

What the C$200 buys you over the C$100 Laifen Air:

  • Scalp Shield, which limits air temperature near the scalp Manufacturer claim
  • A styling and drying suite rather than a plain dryer with attachments Manufacturer claim
  • A somewhat longer Canadian track record — 24 months on sale against Laifen’s newest listings at 4 to 11 months Amazon.ca data

What the extra C$200 over Shark buys with Dyson:

  • Universal voltage on the Travel model, which is a hard functional advantage
  • A Canadian service network and a decade of product history
  • A 5× larger Canadian review base to judge reliability from

Drying performance: Shark vs Dyson

Shark markets the SpeedStyle Pro as “high-velocity,” Dyson as “high-speed digital” — both are describing the same high-airflow, lower-heat approach.

  • Airflow was the most-discussed topic in our entire dataset at 1,585 mentions, and the complaint pattern runs one way: reviewers complain about dryers that are too weak, almost never too powerful Review analysis
  • Shark’s SpeedStyle Pro ranks #13 in the Hair Dryers category, ahead of both Dyson SKUs at #34 and #36 Amazon.ca data
  • That ranking is on 288 estimated units a month against Dyson’s 234 and 182 — Shark is currently outselling both Dyson models in Canada Amazon.ca data

What we cannot tell you. We have not measured airflow or dry time on any of these units. The category’s own marketing language — “high-velocity,” “high-speed,” “professional performance” — has no consistent unit attached to it by any brand, which is exactly why we do not repeat it as fact.

One thing worth noting: Shark’s stronger sales ranking despite a much smaller review base suggests recent momentum rather than a long accumulation. That cuts both ways — it means the product is being discovered, not that it has been proven.

Weight and handling: Shark vs Dyson

Weight is the third most-discussed topic in our dataset at 1,318 mentions, and 73% of that discussion is positive.

  • Dyson Supersonic Travel is explicitly designed as a lighter, more compact variant Manufacturer claim
  • Shark SpeedStyle Pro is a dryer-plus-styling-system, and systems of this type tend to carry more hardware Manufacturer claim
  • Across our dataset, reviewers of step-up and multi-feature dryers frequently note extra weight as the trade-off Review analysis

Why it matters here specifically. If you buy Shark for the styling suite, you will be holding it longer per session than someone who only dries. Weight compounds with session length, and our weight complaints cluster around longer hair and longer sessions.

A note on the FlexStyle confusion. Buyers comparing FlexStyle against a Supersonic are comparing a multi-styler against a dryer, and the weight difference between those two categories is large. Make sure you are comparing the like-for-like pair: SpeedStyle Pro against Supersonic.

Heat and scalp protection: Shark vs Dyson

This is Shark’s clearest feature advantage, and it maps onto a real complaint pattern in our data.

  • Shark SpeedStyle Pro is marketed with Scalp Shield, which limits air temperature near the scalp Manufacturer claim
  • Dyson Supersonic Nural takes a different route with heat sensing that adjusts to distance from the head Manufacturer claim
  • Temperature and overheating generated 590 negative mentions in our dataset — 54% of all heat-related comments were negative Review analysis
  • Reviewers describe dryers that “run too hot on high” and force constant use of the cool button, and in several cases, burns to the scalp or wrist Buyer feedback

The honest read. Scalp protection targets a complaint that genuinely exists in our data. But the severe outcomes we captured — melting plastic, burns, smoke — were hardware failures rather than heat-setting problems. A scalp shield does not protect you from a cord that fails at the handle junction.

For fine hair or a sensitive scalp, this feature is the strongest single argument for choosing Shark over a plain high-speed dryer at the same price.

Noise: Shark vs Dyson

Noise appears in 848 reviews in our dataset, 10.3% of the total, with 33% negative.

  • Neither Shark nor Dyson publishes a measured sound pressure figure at a stated distance Manufacturer claim
  • “Low noise” appears across this category without measurement, including on budget dryers in the same dataset Manufacturer claim
  • Noise was the fourth most-mentioned concern overall, behind airflow, usability and size Review analysis

What we will publish: sound pressure at 30 cm and 1 metre, against a recorded background level, using the same meter for every unit. Until that exists, every quiet claim in this category is unverified — including Shark’s and Dyson’s.

Attachments and styling: Shark vs Dyson

This is the second area where Shark’s feature set is genuinely different rather than just cheaper.

  • SpeedStyle Pro includes an IQ Speed styling and drying suite — the dryer-plus-styling approach rather than a plain dryer Manufacturer claim
  • Dyson Supersonic models use magnetic attachments on a dryer-first platform Manufacturer claim
  • Attachment security generated 186 mentions in our dataset, 57% negative — “the nozzle keeps falling off” and “the concentrator does not stay on” are the recurring phrasings Review analysis
  • One reviewer reported a nozzle that had melted where it sat against the barrel Buyer feedback

If styling is your main use case, the comparison you actually want is Shark FlexStyle against Dyson Airwrap, not SpeedStyle against Supersonic. We cover that pairing separately in our Dyson alternatives guide.

If drying is your main use case, check attachment fit on arrival regardless of which brand you buy — it is a small, cheap thing to verify and a genuinely common complaint.

Travel and storage: Shark vs Dyson

Dyson wins this category clearly.

  • Dyson Supersonic Travel uses universal voltage — usable in Europe, the UK and Australia with only a plug adapter Manufacturer claim
  • The Shark SpeedStyle Pro is not marketed as dual voltage Manufacturer claim
  • Voltage was the single most-discussed topic in our entire dataset at 785 mentions — ahead of noise, weight and price Review analysis

If you travel internationally, the Travel model’s universal voltage is worth real money, because the alternative is buying a second dryer abroad. For cheaper dual-voltage options, see our travel hair dryer guide.

Durability and warranty: Shark vs Dyson

This is where the Shark case is weakest, and it is not Shark’s fault — it is a data problem.

Where Shark sits. At about C$200 it is comfortably inside the over-C$120 band where complaint rates fall to 9.6%. That is a genuine point in its favour.

What we cannot tell you: whether Shark’s 4.4 stars from 64 ratings will hold at 300 ratings. Dyson’s larger Canadian base is more informative, and its service network is a decade old. If you are buying on the strength of reliability evidence, Dyson has more of it — not because Shark has failed, but because Shark has not been around long enough at this volume.

Practical guidance regardless of brand: check the cord strain relief where it enters the handle on arrival. Cord and connector failure accounted for 417 mentions in our dataset, the second most common failure mode after complete stoppage at 601.

Who should buy Shark

Buy the Shark SpeedStyle Pro if:

  • You have a sensitive scalp or fine hair and want the Scalp Shield approach
  • You want a styling and drying suite rather than a plain dryer, but do not want Dyson pricing
  • You want to spend C$200 rather than C$400, and you are comfortable that the reliability record is thin
  • Styling is part of your routine and you want one device rather than two
  • You are buying for home use and do not need dual voltage

Do not buy Shark if:

  • You travel internationally and need universal voltage
  • Proven long-term reliability is your primary criterion
  • You mainly want fast drying under C$150 — the Laifen Air at about C$100 covers that
  • You actually want a multi-styler — that is the FlexStyle, a different product

Check price for the Shark SpeedStyle Pro at Amazon.ca · Read our Dyson alternatives guide

Who should buy Dyson

Buy Dyson if:

  • Universal voltage matters because you travel — the Travel model solves a real problem
  • You want the largest Canadian review base and the longest product history to judge from
  • You want a Canadian service network behind the warranty
  • Your hair is fine, damaged or colour-treated and you want heat sensing rather than a scalp shield
  • A 2× to 3× price premium over Shark is not a meaningful constraint

Do not buy Dyson if:

  • Price is the deciding factor and C$200 is your ceiling
  • Scalp protection is the specific feature you want
  • You are comparing it against FlexStyle — that is an Airwrap-class product, not a dryer

Shark vs Dyson: FAQ

Is Shark as good as Dyson? On features, Shark’s SpeedStyle Pro is competitive — it adds scalp protection and a styling suite. On proven reliability, neither Shark nor Dyson is well documented in our dataset, and Shark has only 64 Canadian ratings against Dyson’s 310 and 125. Dyson has the longer track record and the Canadian service network.

Why is Shark cheaper than Dyson? In Canada the Shark SpeedStyle Pro is about C$200 against about C$400 for the Dyson Supersonic Travel and about C$630 for the Supersonic Nural. The gap is roughly 2× to 3.2× — narrower than the Laifen vs Dyson gap. You are paying less for brand equity and service network rather than for airflow.

What is the difference between Shark FlexStyle and SpeedStyle? They are different product categories. FlexStyle is a multi-styler comparable to the Dyson Airwrap, and it carries the bulk of Shark’s Canadian search volume. SpeedStyle Pro is a high-velocity hair dryer comparable to the Supersonic. Do not compare FlexStyle to a Supersonic — they do different jobs.

How many reviews does the Shark SpeedStyle Pro have in Canada? Only 64 ratings on Amazon.ca as of 2026-10-02, against 310 for the Dyson Supersonic Travel and 125 for the Supersonic Nural. That is a small sample, and it is the single biggest limitation on any Shark recommendation — there are not yet enough long-term Canadian owners to judge reliability.

Does Shark have a scalp protection feature Dyson does not? Yes. The SpeedStyle Pro is marketed with a Scalp Shield feature that limits air temperature near the scalp, which is relevant if you have a sensitive scalp or fine hair. Dyson’s equivalent approach is heat sensing on the Supersonic Nural rather than a scalp-specific shield.

Which is better for travel, Shark or Dyson? Dyson. The Supersonic Travel uses universal voltage, which makes it usable in Europe, the UK and Australia with only a plug adapter. The Shark SpeedStyle Pro is not marketed as dual voltage, so it is a home dryer rather than a travel dryer.

Our verdict on Shark vs Dyson

Shark has the better feature case; Dyson has the better evidence case.

The Shark SpeedStyle Pro at about C$200 is genuinely interesting: it is half the price of a Supersonic, it currently outsells both Dyson models in Canada, and Scalp Shield addresses a complaint that appears 590 times in our review data. If you have a sensitive scalp or want a styling suite without Dyson pricing, it is a reasonable purchase.

What holds it back is not performance — it is that 64 Canadian ratings is not enough to tell you how long it lasts. Dyson’s C$200–430 premium buys a longer track record, a Canadian service network, and universal voltage on the Travel model, and those are concrete things rather than marketing.

Our pick for value: the Shark SpeedStyle Pro. Our pick if you want the most evidence behind the decision: the Dyson Supersonic Travel. And if you simply want fast high-speed drying for the least money, the Laifen Air at about C$100 beats both on price per unit of airflow — see our Laifen vs Dyson comparison.
